obtained.how: the thesis PDF in McGill University's own repository (McGill eScholarship, mcgill.scholaris.ca; handle 20.500.14905/86054), 175 pages. A typewritten thesis whose OCR text layer is badly garbled: every value and quote below was read on the page image

bibliography.checked_against: the title page (PDF p. 1) and the abstract page (PDF p. 2)
bibliography.note: Carlos M. Duarte, 'Biomass and distribution of submerged macrophytes in lakes', PhD thesis, Department of Biology, McGill University, Montreal, May 1987 — all match. The DOI 10.82308/9029 is not a Crossref DOI (show.mjs: not found); it resolves through McGill's repository, as does the handle

claims.claim: Duarte's thesis covers 25 southern Québec and north-eastern US lakes
claims.location: p. 69 (PDF p. 82), ch. III Materials and methods; Table 3.1, p. 72 (PDF p. 85)
claims.quote: The study involved 25 lakes in Québec, New York, and Vermont
claims.conditions: August 1985; recording echosounder, six transects per site from c. 0.7 m depth to the vegetation limit, 187 sites (4–38 per lake), > 8,000 estimates averaged into 1,400 observations by 0.5-m depth class; Table 3.1's lakes lie at about 43.5–46° N (most in southern Québec, plus Lake George and Missisquoi Bay)
depth of maximum colonization of submerged macrophytes against Secchi depth across the 25 lakes (one point per lake), m
as eq. 2; the biomass–depth profile was dome-shaped in every lake

claims.note: 1.9 + 0.63 × 3.5 = 4.105; × 3.9 → 4.357; × 4.5 → 4.735 — the table's 4.11 / 4.36 / 4.74. The bed shares (~83 % / 100 %) come from the model's bed and are not in the source

claims.claim: in Duarte's 25 lakes the shallowest submerged plants grew at 0.75–1.25 m regardless of slope, exposure or transparency, which Duarte attributed to ice scour
claims.quote: this minimum depth is not related to slope, exposure or transparency
claims.conditions: the shallowest depth with submerged vegetation was 0.75–1.25 m; Duarte: the shallow limit 'is probably set by ice scouring'. CAVEAT: the echosounder transects began at c. 0.7 m (p. 69), so the survey could not see plants shallower than that; the 0.75-m end of the range sits at the survey's own start and the data were averaged by 0.5-m depth class
claims.note: the ice-scour reading is Duarte's inference ('probably'), not a measurement

claims.claim: in Lake Memphremagog biomass fell with slope as slope^−0.81
claims.conditions: MSMB = maximum submerged macrophyte biomass (g fresh wt m⁻²; pp. 39, 41 = PDF pp. 52, 54), 44 stations in Lake Memphremagog; slope in m per m; −0.81 was the power transformation that best linearized the relation. The residuals split the data at 2.2 % slope (p. 46), and a separate pair of equations split at 5.3 % (p. 39)
claims.note: strictly an intercept plus a power term (122 + 986·slope^−0.81), not a pure power law

claims.claim: in 25 lakes no plants grew on slopes steeper than ~14.8 %
claims.quote: This critical slope was found to be about 14.8% (Fig. 5)
claims.conditions: submerged biomass was zero beyond the critical slope (302 of the 1,400 site-depth observations); split found by the Breiman et al. (1984) technique; it reduced the overall variance by 13 %

claims.quote: the upper rooting depth in the lake (0.9 m) where wave action is most severe
claims.conditions: Lake Memphremagog fertilization experiment; the plots were set 0.5 m deeper at the start to allow for the normal 0.5-m summer fall in water level
claims.note: here Duarte ties Memphremagog's upper limit to wave action, not ice; the code comment groups it with the ice-scour limit

notes: Not checkable from the thesis: §3.4.4's 'published as Duarte & Kalff 1990' — the thesis cites only 'Duarte and Kalff submitted' (p. 69, for the exposure measure); the published paper would have to be checked separately. The thesis chapter III also gives the deep and shallow multiple regressions (eq. 4, p. 87: below Zmb, biomass^0.33 = −13.0 − 1.6 ln slope − 0.45 ln exposure + 2.3 ln alkalinity + 1.2 ln Si, r² 0.31), with Si from k = 1.47/Secchi (Walker 1982; p. 70). Chapter IV's Memphremagog depth of maximum submerged biomass is 2.6 m (p. 105).
